SEC16A-01.note: Either/or subject: verb agrees with the nearer element 'several of her nestmates' (plural), and 'Ever since' requires present perfect -> have hauled. 'has hauled' attracts anyone agreeing with 'a lone scout' or treating either/or as singular.

SEC16A-02.note: Inverted 'Only in ... has the assumption begun': subject is singular 'assumption', participle 'begun' (beyond four words) needs an auxiliary have, and 'in the decades since' wants present perfect. 'have' attracts via plural 'submersibles'/'vents' just before the blank; 'had' is a tense trap.

SEC16A-03.note: Relative 'that' refers to 'shoots' (plural), and shoots are preserved by someone, so passive plural 'have been preserved'. 'has been preserved' attracts readers who attach 'that' to 'revival' (the head noun whose verb is 'is remarkable').

SEC16A-04.note: Expletive 'there' + delayed compound subject 'both a strip ... and a fragment' (plural), past narrative frame -> were still concealed. 'was still concealed' attracts readers who see only 'a strip' or the intervening singular 'glue'/'binder'.

SEC16A-05.note: Inverted past counterfactual 'Had one researcher not taken...' requires 'would have been dismissed'; 'then' confirms past reference. 'would be dismissed' (mixed conditional) is the strongest distractor; 'will have been' clashes with any conditional.

SEC16A-06.note: Third member of a past-tense series (drifted, lingered, and headed). 'had headed' tempts because of the nearby 'had begun', but it would wrongly place heading out before the gill change.

SEC16A-07.note: Series after a colon whose items contain internal commas must be separated by semicolons. All-commas (A) is the attractive distractor; double colons (B) and the missing comma before 'kefir' (C) are strikeable on sight.

SEC16A-08.convention: Restrictive appositive: the engineer made more than a dozen plates, so the title identifies WHICH plate and should take no commas; a comma before a trailing 'because' clause is permissible in edited prose, making B defensible and C's nonrestrictive pair semantically wrong.
SEC16A-08.note: Every option prints the closing comma after the title, so the key is decided by pairing it (C) - a mark-matching tell. But the passage's 'more than a dozen plates' makes the title restrictive, which argues for no opening comma (B); the item contradicts its own setup. Semicolon (A) and dash/comma mismatch (D) are struck on sight.
SEC16A-08.drop_reason: Key B is right on the restrictive-appositive rule, but every option prints the closing comma after the title, so a lone comma before 'because' sits right next to an apparent comma pair. Pairing that comma gives C, so the printed mark pushes careful test-takers toward the wrong answer, and I missed it cold. The comma before 'because' is optional style, not a convention SAT tests. To fix it, remove the trailing comma from all options (e.g. end the title before a clause that needs no comma), so the item turns only on restrictive vs nonrestrictive.

SEC16B-01.note: Singular subject 'mortar' (the 'including...' phrase does not add to it) takes an active verb whose object is 'the hairline cracks' after the interrupter -> repeatedly seals. 'repeatedly seal' attracts via 'fragments'; passive options leave 'the hairline cracks' stranded.

SEC16B-02.note: Fraction of a mass noun ('two-thirds of the buried carbon') takes a singular verb, and carbon is carried in, so passive 'was actually brought'. 'were' attracts via 'two-thirds'; 'into' with no object makes the active forms fail.

SEC16B-03.note: Postpositive 'each' after a plural subject ('The two notebooks ... each') leaves the verb plural; notebooks are digitized by volunteers, so passive 'are now being digitized'. 'is' attracts via 'each'; active forms lack an object.

SEC16B-04.note: A participial phrase of result after the comma ('leaving riverside towns') attaches to the clause; finite 'left'/'had left' would be an unjoined third verb with a tense shift. 'having left' attracts as a participle but implies prior action.

SEC16B-05.note: Future-in-the-past after past reporting verb 'assured' -> would keep out; the wall has since been built and failed, so 'will' (no backshift) is unavailable. 'had kept out' tempts as a backshift but reverses time order.

SEC16B-06.note: The age is the thing determined, so passive with general-ability modal: 'can be determined'. 'can determine' attracts as the right modal but has no object; 'had been determined' clashes with the present generalization.

SEC16B-07.note: Complete clause followed by a noun phrase that specifies 'a feature' -> colon. Semicolon (A) is the strongest distractor, wrong because 'deep notches ... that give...' is not an independent clause; a comma (C) would attach the appositive to 'magnification'.

SEC16B-08.note: A list fronted before a summarizing clause ('any one of these conditions...') is joined by a dash; the period (A) leaves the list a fragment, the comma (B) is a splice-like misjoin. 'any one of these' after the blank cues the summarizing dash.

tells: Passive wins whenever a number x voice grid is offered with no object after the blank: A-03, B-02, B-03, B-06 all key the passive; only B-01 (where an object 'the hairline cracks' follows the interrupter) keys active. A test-taker who learns 'pick passive when nothing follows the verb' gets 4 of 5 without agreement reasoning.
A-08: every option prints the closing comma, so the key is chosen by pairing it (C) - pure mark-matching, and it contradicts the restrictive reading the passage sets up.

In agreement items the key is consistently the one NOT matching the noun printed immediately before the blank (A-01 'nestmates' is the exception that matches; A-02 'vents'->has, A-03 'revival' head vs 'shoots', A-04 'binder'->were, B-01 'fragments'->seals, B-02 'carbon' ok but 'two-thirds' trap, B-03 'each'->are). Heavy reliance on attraction traps is itself a recognisable pattern: 'distrust the nearest noun' solves most of A-02, A-04, B-01, B-03.
Punctuation items: the key is the stronger/less common mark in 3 of 3 non-A-08 items (A-07 semicolons, B-07 colon, B-08 dash); the plain comma option never wins in this batch.
summary.near_duplicate_notes: A-03/B-03/B-01/B-02 share the singular/plural x active/passive 2x2 option grid; A-02/A-04 are both inverted-subject agreement (only-inversion, there-expletive); A-06/B-04 both pick a verb form in the slot after a comma in a past narrative series; A-05/B-05 both are would-forms (conditional / future-in-past).

phase2_note: Grader d agreed with the key on 15 of 16 items cold. The miss is A-08 (my C vs key B). On reading the explanation, B is correct (the title is restrictive among a dozen plates), but the fixed closing comma makes C look like a paired comma, so I recommend dropping or re-authoring A-08. All 16 explanations are coherent and reject each distractor correctly. Batch-level concern (not a per-item drop): the passive key wins in 4 of the 5 number x voice grids (A-03, B-02, B-03, B-06), and those items share one template.
